sources.title: Sugita Genpaku (Q1385286), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-18): English label 'Sugita Genpaku', description 'Japanese scholar', Japanese label 杉田玄白, Korean label 스기타 겐파쿠, born 1733-10-20, died 1817-06-01, a human, citizen of Japan. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Japanese reference-work entries on Sugita Genpaku as collected on Kotobank (read in full, in Japanese): the Nippon Encyclopedia (Nipponica) article by Katagiri Kazuo (2016), the Heibonsha World Encyclopedia article by Muneta Hajime, and the Britannica International short entry. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: a physician of the Obama domain who, after watching a dissection at the Kozukappara execution ground on 4 March 1771 with Maeno Ryotaku and Nakagawa Jun'an and finding the Dutch anatomy book accurate, began translating it (Maeno as the leader of the work per the Heibonsha entry) and published it in 1774 as Kaitai Shinsho, the first full-scale translation of a Western medical book in Edo and the start of the rise of Dutch studies; he then trained many pupils (Otsuki Gentaku, Udagawa Genshin and others) through his school Tenshinro, ran a regular research meeting, collected Dutch books for pupils' use, spread medical knowledge through essays such as Keiei Yawa, wrote critical essays on politics and society, painted, wrote poetry and died in 1817 aged 85. Scholarly encyclopedia entries, admiring but factual.

National Diet Library, Japan, 'Japan-Netherlands Exchange in the Edo Period', Part 2 'Activities of Dutch Studies' (page read) and the library's catalogue record for the 1774 Kaitai Shinsho (page read): credits Sugita Genpaku, Maeno Ryotaku, Nakagawa Jun'an and Katsuragawa Hoshu as translators and Odano Naotake as illustrator; says the translation took from 1771 to 1774 and that its difficulty is described in Genpaku's memoir Rangaku Kotohajime (completed 1815, first printed in 1869 through Fukuzawa Yukichi and Sugita Renkei); says Maeno Ryotaku, the best Dutch scholar of the group, refused to have his name listed as a translator; describes the Sugita family as physicians of the Obama domain and Genpaku as teacher of Otsuki Gentaku and others at the private school Tenshinro. National library exhibition text, factual.

Japan Search (National Diet Library), 'Genpaku Sugita' biography page (read in English): says he studied surgery under Nishi Gentetsu and Chinese learning under Miyase Ryumon, attended the Kozukappara autopsy in 1771, and after three years' work published Kaitai Shinsho in 1774; lists his friendship with Hiraga Gennai (he is said to have erected Gennai's gravestone), his essays (Keiei Yawa, Nochimi Gusa, Yaso Dokugo), the 1773 sample sheet Kaitai Yakuzu issued before the printing, the revision Chotei Kaitai Shinsho that Otsuki Gentaku made at Genpaku's order (completed 1798, printed 1826), and his son Rikkei and grandson Seikei as physician-translators. National-library catalogue page, factual.

Jeremy Norman, 'Kaitai Shinsho: the first book on Western medicine and science published in Japanese', History of Information (page read): gives S. Kuriyama's 1992 assessment that the book began both the modern transformation of Japanese medicine (introducing the idea of learning the body by visual inspection in dissection) and the rise of Dutch studies; notes that the book was drawn largely from Gerard Dicten's 1773 Dutch edition of Kulmus's tables, with the title page copied from Valverde and the last four woodcuts from Bidloo; reports, on Genpaku's own account, that he and two other students of Dutch medicine saw a criminal's body dissected in 1771 and decided to translate the book, and that it sold out almost at once and went through many editions. Rare-book dealer's reference page quoting a scholar; the dissection story is Genpaku's own account.

Lewis Bremner, 'The Magic Lantern as a Lens for Observing the Eye in Tokugawa Japan: Technology, translation, and the Rangaku movement', Modern Asian Studies 54(3), 2019 (Cambridge University Press; article text read): independent scholarship that describes Sugita and the other early Dutch-studies figures as concluding, under the influence of the School of Ancient Medicine, that direct observation was the only sound basis for knowledge; that Kaitai Shinsho followed its Dutch source closely but omitted all of Kulmus's footnotes and added four illustrations from Bidloo; that Sugita consulted a wide range of Dutch and Chinese texts and combined critical analysis with observation; and that Otsuki Gentaku, his pupil, later produced the revised Chotei Kaitai Shinsho (1826). Peer-reviewed article in which Sugita is a supporting figure.

More Than Tokyo, 'Sugita Genpaku: remarkable Edo-era pioneer of human anatomy' (travel-history blog, page read in full): a popular retelling drawn mainly from Genpaku's own memoir Rangaku Kotohajime, so it is largely his own account: obtaining a Dutch anatomy book with money from his lord, the 1771 dissection and his remark that he was ashamed not to know the structure of the body, the group's slow work on the Dutch text with Maeno's limited Dutch and a dictionary, the 1772 visit to the Nagasaki delegation, the 1773 booklet Kaitai Yakuzu that named only Obama-domain men so as to protect Maeno, the gift of copies to the shogun's senior councillor, the imperial household and the shogun before the 1774 publication, Maeno's refusal to be credited, and a quotation from Keiei Yawa denying any real difference between emperor and commoner. Not independent of the memoir; blog source.

Wikipedia, 'Kaitai Shinsho' (English article, read for orientation): translation work centred on Maeno Ryotaku, with Sugita adding notes; the 1773 Kaitai Yakuzu flyer issued to gauge the authorities' response; the dedication by the interpreter Yoshio Kogyu. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Japanese Wiki Corpus, 'Sugita Genpaku' (English translation of the Japanese Wikipedia article, read for orientation): career dates, the 1765 meeting with the Nagasaki interpreter Nishi Zensaburo who advised him against learning Dutch, his 1805 audience with the shogun and 1807 retirement from the domain post. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

curiosity.rationale: [src_sugita_kotobank, src_sugita_bremner, src_sugita_norman | 1755-1771 | reference encyclopedias, scholarly article, rare-book reference] The Heibonsha entry says that, dissatisfied with the surgery he had learned, he went through Chinese surgical texts, then visited the Dutch physicians and interpreters at the Nagasakiya inn in Edo to watch treatment and borrow original surgical books whose fine plates he copied; the Nipponica entry adds that he questioned the Dutch head and the interpreter Yoshio Kogyu about Dutch surgery before obtaining the Dutch anatomy book, and the 1771 dissection followed. Bremner describes him as consulting a wide range of Dutch and Chinese texts. CONCENTRATION: the visits and the 'ashamed' remark are mostly his own memoir as retold; lowered from 72 / 0.56 to 68 / 0.52.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_sugita_kotobank, src_sugita_jpsearch, src_sugita_ndl, src_sugita_mtt | 1771-1807 | reference encyclopedias, national-library pages, blog] The Nipponica entry calls him the driving force behind getting the translation published; the Heibonsha entry has the group resolving to translate the day after the dissection; the National Diet Library pages record the 1773 sample sheet issued ahead of the printing; the blog (from his own memoir) adds that he gave copies to the shogun's senior councillor and the shogun. He also ran a school and collected Dutch books for pupils. Maeno Ryotaku, not Genpaku, led the translating, so the initiative lies in promotion and organisation. CONCENTRATION: the promotion details rest on his own memoir; lowered from 72 / 0.58 to 70 / 0.54.

persistence.rationale: [src_sugita_ndl, src_sugita_kotobank, src_sugita_jpsearch, src_sugita_norman | 1771-1774 | national-library pages, reference encyclopedias, rare-book reference] The National Diet Library gives the translation as taking from 1771 to 1774 and says the difficulty is told in his memoir; the Heibonsha entry gives three years and the Nipponica entry four; Japan Search says three years of hard work. The sources differ on the length (one reference page says two years). The nature of the difficulty rests on his own memoir. CONCENTRATION: multi-year effort is independently stated, but the hardship narrative is self-report; lowered from 68 / 0.54 to 66 / 0.50.

collaboration.rationale: [src_sugita_ndl, src_sugita_kotobank, src_sugita_mtt | 1771-1774 | national-library pages, reference encyclopedias, blog] The National Diet Library credits four translators and the illustrator Odano Naotake; the Heibonsha entry says the group worked with Maeno Ryotaku as its leader and Genpaku as one of the comrades; the memoir-derived blog says the 1773 booklet carried only Obama-domain names to protect Maeno and that Maeno declined credit. Genpaku also arranged his friend Hiraga Gennai's grave (Japan Search). Shared-credit risk: the work was a group effort, and how Genpaku divided it is little described. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.52 to 62 / 0.48 (evidence type relabelled inference) because credit for the translation is shared and the protection story is his own.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_sugita_kotobank, src_sugita_bremner, src_sugita_jpsearch, src_sugita_mtt | 1754-1798 | reference encyclopedias, scholarly article, national-library page, blog] The Heibonsha entry says he left the surgery he had trained in as inadequate and moved to Dutch methods; after the dissection he confirmed the Dutch plates were accurate (the 'ashamed' remark is his own account in the memoir via the blog); Bremner describes early Dutch-studies figures like him as treating direct observation as the only sound basis for knowledge; Japan Search says Otsuki Gentaku revised Kaitai Shinsho at Genpaku's order (completed 1798). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.46 (relabelled inference) because the change of mind is told chiefly in his memoir and the revision order rests on one catalogue page.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_sugita_kotobank, src_sugita_ndl, src_sugita_jpsearch | 1774-1817 | reference encyclopedias, national-library pages] The Nipponica entry says he spread medical knowledge through essays such as Keiei Yawa and Yojo Shichifuka, ran the school Tenshinro between his duties to his lord and his patients, trained many pupils (Otsuki Gentaku, Sugita Hakugen, Udagawa Genshin) and lent Dutch books to them; the National Diet Library names Tenshinro and its pupils. The activity is well documented, but the motive is read from the activity and the entries are admiring. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.52 to 64 / 0.48 (relabelled inference) because the evidence is institutional praise of a teaching record rather than a described motive.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_sugita_jpsearch, src_sugita_kotobank, src_sugita_mtt | 1773-1774 | national-library page, reference encyclopedia, blog] Japan Search records the 1773 sample sheet Kaitai Yakuzu, a five-sheet sample issued about a year before the printing, and the Heibonsha entry calls Kaitai Shinsho the first translation to state its method and policy for translating a foreign book. The blog (from his memoir) says the sample was meant to test reception. A staged release is documented; the reasoning behind it comes from his own account.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_sugita_kotobank, src_sugita_mtt | 1773-1810 | reference encyclopedias, blog] The Nipponica entry lists essays in which he set out his own views on politics and society (Atomigusa, Yaso Dokugo and others) in addition to medical essays, and the blog quotes a passage from Keiei Yawa denying any real difference of rank between emperor and commoner. The essays are named but not analysed in the sources read; the quotation is from one blog.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_sugita_kotobank, src_sugita_ndl | 1774-1817 | reference encyclopedias, national-library page] The Nipponica entry records that he ran Tenshinro and held a regular research meeting (a disease-theory society) in rotating members' houses, according to his diary, and passed the school to an adopted son; the National Diet Library names the school and its pupils. The role as head of a school is documented; his style of leading is not described.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_sugita_kotobank | 1750s-1817 | reference encyclopedia] Beyond medicine and Dutch translation the Nipponica entry records that he learned linked-verse poetry, wrote verse, associated with Western-style painters (Soshiseki, Ishikawa Tairo) and painted, including a large many-crane picture, and wrote political and social essays. Single-source breadth, with medicine at the centre; no source treats it as a distinct trait.

portrait.source: Woodblock-printed portrait captioned 鷧斎杉田先生肖像 ('Portrait of Master Sugita Isai') and signed 大浪寫 (Ishikawa Tairo), the frontispiece of the first volume of Sugita Genpaku's Keiei Yawa (Edo, 1810, Shotokyo edition), with the printed note on the next page (dated the seventh month of Kogo, 1810, signed by his son Kin) saying that Sugita, now 78, asked Ishikawa Tairo to copy his true likeness. Digital scan of the Kano Collection copy at Tohoku University Main Library (record 10010000024388, scan THKK-90004-00003, 3888 x 2571 two-page spread). The file is a crop of the portrait leaf, converted to greyscale and downscaled to 881 x 1200 with no upscaling.
portrait.license: Public domain: woodblock print published in Edo in 1810 after a likeness by Ishikawa Tairo (died 1818); Tohoku University Main Library's terms of use for its expired-copyright materials permit reproduction, modification and distribution, commercial or not, with the title and 'Held by Tohoku University Main Library' credited, and the item's metadata marks secondary use as CC BY
portrait.attribution: Frontispiece portrait of Sugita Genpaku (Isai) by Ishikawa Tairo, in Keiei Yawa (1810), Kano Collection (Held by Tohoku University Main Library), digital scan THKK-90004.
portrait.creator: Ishikawa Tairo (drawn from the sitter); block-printed for the Shotokyo edition of Keiei Yawa

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (Stage B) / REPLACED. Lead was Commons 'Sugita Genpaku.jpg' (Ishikawa Tairo portrait, Waseda University Library, Bunko 08 A0252, 1187 x 1415, PD-Art/PD-Japan on Commons). The lead did NOT survive: Waseda's holder record is bot-walled (archive.wul.waseda.ac.jp returned 403 and the kotenseki page 503 maintenance in plain fetch and in a browser), and the one Waseda page that could be read (a 2016 news item on its Kotenseki database) states that use of the database's materials on websites, in publications and exhibitions without permission is strictly prohibited, a reuse restriction that overrides the Commons PD template. Not used. REPLACEMENT: the frontispiece of Sugita's own Keiei Yawa (1810), read as a Tohoku University Main Library digital scan (Kano Collection, 3888 x 2571): printed caption 'Portrait of Master Sugita Isai', Tairo's signature, and the next page's note by his son Kin (seventh month 1810) saying Sugita at 78 asked Ishikawa Tairo to copy his true likeness. Holder terms read: Tohoku's use-of-materials page allows free use of expired-copyright items with credit; item metadata says secondary use CC BY. KIND likeness (a print after a portrait from the sitter's lifetime, commissioned by him). The cropped file is greyscale, downscaled to 881 x 1200, no upscaling. Caveats: the print is a woodcut after Tairo's painting, not the painting itself; the Tohoku catalogue note says 'portrait included'; CC BY metadata applies to the scan, the underlying work is public domain by age. IDENTITY: QID Q1385286 verified live 2026-11-18 (label 'Sugita Genpaku', ja 杉田玄白, ko 스기타 겐파쿠, born 1733-10-20, died 1817-06-01, human, Japan). REGION east_asia (Japanese precedent Hiraga Gennai, Ino Tadataka). ERA early_modern (precedent Hiraga Gennai). ZERO POLITICS: his political essays are context, one is cited only as independent thinking and no political position is scored. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (dated publications, institutions, a school with named pupils; his own memoir Rangaku Kotohajime is the main source for the translation story and is treated as self-report). Sparse by design (10 rows). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Nipponica (Katagiri Kazuo) and Heibonsha World Encyclopedia (Muneta Hajime) entries on Kotobank. NOT OPENED: the memoir itself (Matsumoto translation / Japanese text), Katagiri's 1971 biography, Kuriyama's essay (quoted via the History of Information page). CONFLICTS NOT CARDED: translation length (two years per one reference page, three to four years per the encyclopedias and National Diet Library), dissection place (Odawara per a school page, Kozukappara per scholarship), whether Maeno or Sugita should be called the translator (Maeno led, per Heibonsha; Sugita is credited on the book). KO NAME: 스기타 겐파쿠 is the Wikidata Korean label. HANDBACK: see TGI-r68-scratch handback/sugita-genpaku.json.
